day-1.t: Day 1 — Plan the report before you touch Excel

b.v: Today's goal

v: Write down who will read your report and what decision they must make
Choose the three questions the dashboard must answer
Draw a rough layout on paper and keep it next to your keyboard

b.v: About 20 minutes. A pen, one sheet of paper and Excel open on the sample data.

Most bad dashboards are not bad because of formulas. They are bad because nobody decided what the reader needs. A dashboard is not a place to show everything you have. It is a place to show the few numbers that change a decision.
1) Name the reader and the decision

Write one sentence: 'The shop owner will use this to decide which city needs a second salesperson.' If you cannot write that sentence, you are not ready to build. The reader decides the level of detail — an owner wants city totals, a supervisor wants salesperson totals.
Write this on paper:|Reader: who opens the file, and how often|Decision: what they will do differently after reading it|Detail level: total only, or total per city, per person, per product
2) Pick the three questions
Three questions is a good limit for one screen. More than that and the reader stops reading. Keep the questions in the language the reader uses, not in spreadsheet words.

v: How much did we sell this month, against the target?
Which city is growing and which is falling?
Which product brings the most money, not just the most units?

b.v: 3) Sketch the layout

Draw boxes on paper: a title strip, three small number cards on top, one chart in the middle, one table at the bottom. This sketch becomes your cell map later, so you never move things around ten times.

v.cap: The data you will report on all course. Type it into a new sheet and save the file as sales-dashboard.xlsx.

b.v: The Total column gives 1800, 2000, 2100, 3000 and 2250. Add them and you get Rs 11,150. Keep that number in your head — every pivot and chart you build later must add up to the same Rs 11,150. If it does not, something is wrong.
The most common beginner mistake is to start with colours and boxes. You spend an hour making it pretty, then discover the reader wanted a different question answered. Paper first, always.
Practice

Type the five rows above into a sheet named Data. In column H use =F2*G2 and fill down. Check that H7 (or wherever your total sits) shows 11150 when you sum column H. Then draw your three-box layout on paper and write the three questions under it.

day-2.t: Day 2 — Clean messy data into one table

b.v: Today's goal

v: Turn a messy sheet into one clean table with one header row
Remove blank rows, merged cells and double spaces
Fix text that looks like a number but is stored as text

b.v: About 20 minutes. Work on a copy of the file, never on the original.

Every PivotTable, every chart and every formula in this course needs one thing: a rectangle of data with one header row, no blank rows inside, and no merged cells. Roughly eighty percent of dashboard pain happens here, before any analysis.
1) Make it one rectangle

Delete the title rows above the header, unmerge merged cells, and delete empty rows and empty columns inside the data. If someone added a subtotal row in the middle, delete it — the PivotTable will make its own totals.

Clean the block:|Select the whole range and press Ctrl+H|Find two spaces, replace with one space, and repeat until nothing changes|Delete rows where the Order ID is empty|Select the data and press Ctrl+T to make it a real Table

v: Ctrl+T = make a Table, which grows automatically when you add rows
Trim spaces = remove hidden spaces at the start or end of text
Text stored as number = a number Excel treats as a word, so sums ignore it

b.v: 2) Fix numbers and dates
A number that is left-aligned in the cell is usually text. It may also have a space, an apostrophe or a comma inside it. Dates typed as text sort wrongly and break month grouping.

Repair a column of fake numbers:|Select the column|Data, then Text to Columns, then Finish — this re-reads each cell as a number|If it still fails, use =VALUE(TRIM(A2)) in a helper column and paste the results back as values|For dates, use Data, then Text to Columns, and choose the correct date format on the third screen
3) Add the helper columns you will need
Add columns for Month and for Line Total. A month column such as Jan-2026 lets you group by month later without fighting Excel's date grouping. A line total column keeps every later sum simple.

v.cap: Cleaned data with two helper columns added at the end

b.v: Do not delete the original rows after cleaning. Keep a sheet called Raw with the untouched data. When a total looks strange three weeks later, you need the original to check against.
Practice

Take any messy sheet you already have — a WhatsApp order list, a shop register, a school fee sheet. Make it one Table with one header row, remove every blank row and merged cell, add a Month helper column, and confirm that a SUM of your amount column matches the total you know by hand.
Today's goal

v: Insert your first PivotTable from the clean Table
Put fields in Rows, Columns and Values on purpose
Change the value from Count to Sum and check the total

b.v: About 20 minutes. Keep the clean Table from Day 2 open.

A PivotTable takes many rows and squeezes them into a small summary. You do not write a formula. You drag a field into a box and Excel groups the rows for you. This is the single most useful tool in this course.
1) Insert it correctly

Click one cell inside your Table, then Insert, then PivotTable. Choose New Worksheet, not an existing cell — a PivotTable needs empty space around it. Excel will pick up the whole Table because it is a real Table.
Insert the pivot:|Click any cell inside the data Table|Insert, then PivotTable, then OK|Drag City into the Rows box|Drag Line Total into the Values box
2) Fix the Count problem
If your Values box says Count of Line Total, Excel found text or blanks in that column. Go back to Day 2 and fix the column. To change it: right-click the value, choose Summarize Values By, then Sum.

v.cap: What the finished pivot looks like. Sum of Line Total by City, and the grand total must match 11150.

b.v: Check the arithmetic yourself: Karachi is 2000 + 2250 = 4250. Lahore is 1800 + 2100 = 3900. Multan is 3000. The three add to 11,150, exactly the number from Day 1. If your grand total is different, your data has a duplicate row or a text number.
3) Add a second view

Copy the PivotTable sheet, then change the Rows field from City to Salesperson. Now you have two summaries without retyping anything. Use the Refresh button on the PivotTable tab after you add new sales rows.

v: Refresh = re-read the data after it changed. A pivot does not update itself the moment you edit a row
Rows box = the words you want down the left side
Values box = the numbers you want added up

b.v: Never type inside a PivotTable to 'fix' a number. The next refresh wipes it. If a number is wrong, the data is wrong — fix the data.
Practice

Build three PivotTables from your Table: total by City, total by Salesperson, and total by Product. Write all three grand totals on paper. All three must be 11,150. Save the file as sales-dashboard.xlsx.

day-4.t: Day 4 — Slicers, timelines and one-click filtering

b.v: Today's goal

v: Add a slicer so the reader filters by city with one click
Connect one slicer to several PivotTables at once
Add a timeline for dates and set a default view

b.v: About 20 minutes. Two PivotTables from Day 3 ready.
A filter dropdown is hidden. A slicer is visible. That difference matters: the reader can see the slicer buttons and understands that the report is interactive, without being taught.
1) Add your first slicer
Click inside a PivotTable, then PivotTable Analyze, then Insert Slicer. Tick City. A floating panel of city buttons appears. Clicking Lahore filters every number in that pivot instantly.

Add and tidy a slicer:|Click inside the PivotTable|PivotTable Analyze, then Insert Slicer, then tick City|Drag the slicer above the pivot and resize it|In Slicer settings, set the number of columns so all cities show in one row
2) Connect one slicer to many pivots

Right-click the slicer, choose Report Connections, and tick every PivotTable that should follow it. This is how a dashboard stays consistent: one click moves all the numbers together, so the reader never sees two different filters on one screen.

v: Report Connections = the list of pivots a slicer controls
Timeline = a date slider instead of buttons, best for months and years
Clear filter = the funnel icon with a red cross, resets the slicer

b.v: 3) Set a sensible default

A dashboard should open showing something meaningful. Select all cities by default, and use a timeline that covers the full year. Do not leave a slicer clicked on one city — the next reader will think sales collapsed.

v.cap: Same pivot, filtered by the slicer to Lahore only

b.v: With Lahore selected, the grand total drops from 11,150 to 3,900. That is correct: only two Lahore orders exist, 1800 and 2100. A reader who forgets a filter is on will misread the whole page, which is why the next lesson puts the filter state on the page in words.
If a slicer does not affect a chart, the chart is not connected to that pivot. Use Report Connections. Do not build a second slicer and hope.
Practice

Add a City slicer and connect it to all three PivotTables from Day 3. Click Karachi and write down the three totals you see. Then click the clear-filter icon and confirm every pivot returns to 11,150.

day-5.t: Day 5 — Charts that lie, and charts that tell the truth

b.v: Today's goal

v: Spot the four common ways a chart misleads
Pick the right chart type for the question
Build a clean column chart and a line chart from your pivots

b.v: About 20 minutes. Read every point slowly — this lesson protects your reputation.

A chart is an argument made of shapes. The same numbers can look like a disaster or a triumph depending on the axis, the colours and the chart type. If you build an honest chart you are trusted. If you build a lying one, people find out.
1) The four lies
These are the tricks you will see in other people's reports, and the mistakes beginners make by accident.

v: Cut axis = a column chart whose vertical axis starts at 900 instead of 0, so a small change looks huge
Cherry-picked period = comparing a good month against a bad month and calling it a trend
Wrong chart = a pie with nine slices, which no human can read
Double axis = two lines on two different scales, drawn so they appear to cross

b.v: 2) Choose the chart by the question

The question decides the chart, not your taste. Categories compared to each other need a column chart. Change over time needs a line chart. One number against a target needs a single big card, not a chart at all.

v: Compare cities = column chart, sorted largest to smallest
Change over months = line chart
Share of a whole, with 3 to 5 parts = pie or doughnut, otherwise a bar chart
One number with a target = a big number card

v.cap: The chart data, sorted. Karachi 4250, Lahore 3900, Multan 3000. Total 11150.

b.v: 3) Build two clean charts

Click inside the City pivot, then Insert, then a clustered column chart. Delete the gridlines, keep the value axis starting at zero, and put the number on top of each column with Data Labels, Outside End.

Build the column chart:|Click inside the pivot|Insert, then Column chart, then Clustered Column|Right-click the vertical axis, Format Axis, and confirm the minimum is 0|Add Data Labels, Outside End|Delete the legend and the gridlines|Change the title to something a human says, such as Sales by city, January 2026
Do not use 3D charts, shadows or gradients. They add nothing and they make the bars harder to compare. A flat, plain chart is the professional choice.
Practice

Build the sorted column chart for the three cities and one line chart of monthly totals. Give both charts a plain English title that states the finding, for example Karachi leads with Rs 4,250. Then take one chart from a report you already have and write down which of the four lies it uses.
Today's goal

v: Choose three KPIs and write the exact formula for each
Build a number card with a target and a percentage
Add a simple status colour with a formula, not by hand

b.v: About 20 minutes. Keep your numbers and a calculator nearby.
KPI means key performance indicator: the few numbers that tell you if the business is on track. If everything is a KPI, nothing is. Three is plenty for one screen.
1) Define each KPI in words
A KPI that cannot be explained in one sentence will be argued about forever. Write the definition, the period and the target next to the number, in small grey text.

v: Sales this month = the sum of all order totals in the month
Average order value = sales divided by the number of orders
Target hit = sales divided by the target, shown as a percentage

v.cap: A three-KPI strip. Target is a typed assumption, everything else is a formula.

b.v: Run the numbers. Sales are 11,150 against a 15,000 target, so that card says Behind. Orders are 5 against 6, also Behind. Average order value is 11,150 divided by 5, which is 2,230 against a 2,500 target, Behind again. Three honest red cards are more useful than one green one.
2) Make the card readable

A card is three lines: a small grey label, a big bold number, and a small line saying against target. Merge a few cells, set the number format to Rs with no decimals, and make the value font about 28 point.

Build one card:|Merge B2 to C3 for the big number|Type the formula =SUM(Data!H2:H6) in it|Format as currency with zero decimals|Put the label Sales this month in B1 in grey 10 point|Put the target line in B4 as small grey text
3) Let a formula choose the colour
Do not colour cells by hand — you will forget to update them. Use conditional formatting on the percentage cell so the colour follows the number, and it stays right every month.

v: =IF(B2>=C2,"On track","Behind") = a formula that returns a word instead of a number
Conditional formatting = a rule that changes colour when a cell meets a condition
Assumption = a number you typed, such as a target, which you should list separately

b.v: Never mix a typed number into a formula, such as =B2/15000. Put the target in its own cell so next month you change one cell, not twenty formulas.
Practice

Build the three-KPI strip shown above on a new sheet called Dashboard. Check that the sales card reads 11,150 and 2,230 for average order value. Then change the target cell to 10,000 and confirm all three cards switch to On track without you touching a colour.

day-7.t: Day 7 — Layout rules and named ranges

b.v: Today's goal

v: Follow five layout rules that make any dashboard easy to read
Create named ranges so formulas read like sentences
Set up a print area and a fixed grid

b.v: About 20 minutes. Work in View, then Page Break Preview so you can see the page edges.

Layout is not decoration. A reader's eye moves in a pattern: top left first, then across, then down. If your most important number sits bottom right, it will be missed. These rules cost nothing and change everything.
1) The five rules

v: Top to bottom = summary first, detail last
One screen = if the reader must scroll to understand one idea, split it into two pages
White space = gaps between groups, not borders everywhere
One accent colour = green for good, red for behind, grey for everything else
Align left = numbers right-aligned, text left-aligned, never centred in a table

b.v: Turn off gridlines on the dashboard sheet. They add a hundred faint lines that compete with your data. View, then untick Gridlines.
2) Name your ranges
A named range gives a cell or a block a word instead of an address. =SUM(SalesAmount) is easier to check than =SUM(Data!H2:H500), especially when someone else reads it six months later.

Create a named range:|Select the cells, for example Data!H2:H6|Click the Name Box on the left of the formula bar|Type the name with no spaces, such as SalesAmount|Press Enter, then use =SUM(SalesAmount) anywhere in the workbook

v.cap: The same dashboard using names. Total is still 11150.

b.v: Names must start with a letter and contain no spaces. A name that looks like a cell address, such as A1, is rejected. Use Sales_Amount or SalesAmount.
3) Set the grid and the print area

Turn on Page Layout view and set column widths in round numbers, such as 2 for a spacer column and 14 for a card. Then mark the print area so the file prints on one page without cutting a chart in half.

v: Print area = the exact block that will print
Fit to one page = scales the sheet down to fit the paper width
Freeze panes = keeps the header row visible while scrolling long data

b.v: A dashboard that prints across three pages, with the KPI cards on page one and the chart on page three, looks careless in a meeting. Set the print area today, not the night before.
Practice

Create two named ranges, SalesAmount and TargetMonth. Rebuild your three KPI cards using the names only. Turn off gridlines. Then set the print area to your whole dashboard and use Fit to one page wide, and look at the print preview.

day-8.t: Day 8 — Conditional formatting that guides the eye

b.v: Today's goal

v: Use data bars, colour scales and icon sets in the right place
Write a formula-based rule for a whole row
Avoid the two formatting mistakes that hide data

b.v: About 20 minutes. One table and one pivot open.

Conditional formatting changes a cell's look when its value meets a rule. Used well, the reader sees the problem before reading any number. Used badly, it turns the sheet into a traffic light with no meaning.
1) The three built-in types

v: Data bar = a small bar inside the cell, good for comparing sizes in a column
Colour scale = a gradient from low to high, good for a grid of numbers, weak for exact reading
Icon set = arrows or flags, good for three to five clear levels and nothing more

b.v: On a pivot of sales by salesperson, a data bar is the best choice: the reader compares lengths instantly. A three-colour scale on the same column adds noise, because the middle values get a muddy colour that means nothing.
2) A rule that colours a whole row
Select the whole table, then Home, Conditional Formatting, New Rule, Use a formula. The formula must be written for the top-left cell of the selection and must use the right dollar signs.

Highlight rows behind target:|Select A2:H6|Home, Conditional Formatting, New Rule, Use a formula|Type =$H2<1000 and choose a light red fill|Click OK, then check that each whole row is coloured, not just one cell

v.cap: Rows under Rs 1,000 would highlight with the rule above

b.v: Every row here is above 1,000, so nothing highlights. That is a useful test: if the whole sheet turns red, your dollar signs are wrong. =$H2 locks the column but lets the row move down. =H$2 does the opposite.
3) Two mistakes to avoid

First, do not use red and green as the only signal — about one in twelve men cannot tell them apart. Add an arrow or a word. Second, do not colour the text the same shade as the fill, because the number disappears.
Do not format an entire column with a rule that covers a million empty rows. It slows the file and paints empty space. Limit the rule to your actual data, or to the Table, which sizes itself.
Practice

Add a data bar to the Sales column of your city pivot. Then add a formula rule to your data Table that highlights any row where Units is below 5. Test it by temporarily changing one unit value to 3, then change it back.

day-9.t: Day 9 — Build the sales dashboard step by step

b.v: Today's goal

v: Assemble one screen using everything from the last eight days
Connect every object to the same data and the same slicer
Check the totals one last time before showing anyone

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is the build lesson, so take your time.
A dashboard is only finished when a stranger can open it, click one button, and understand the story. Today you build that screen, and then you test it like a stranger would.
1) Lay out the grid
Open a new sheet called Dashboard. Set columns A and N as narrow spacers of width 2. Use rows 2 to 4 for the title strip and rows 6 to 9 for the three KPI cards.

Place the objects:|Title in B2, merged across to M2|Three KPI cards in B6, F6 and J6, each about three columns wide|Slicer for City in B11|Column chart of sales by city in B14|Table of top products in H14
2) Connect and test
Every pivot and chart on this sheet must come from the same Table, and every slicer must be connected to all of them. Then test one click and check the arithmetic by hand.

v.cap: The finished screen with no filter applied. Sales 11150, orders 5, average 2230.

b.v: Product totals from the same five rows: Notebook 12 + 20 + 15 = 47 units, and 47 times 150 is 7,050. Pen pack 8 units, 2,000. Stapler 3 units, 2,100. The three add to 11,150, which matches the KPI card. When three different objects agree, you can trust the file.
3) The stranger test

v: Hand the laptop to someone who has not seen the file and say nothing
Watch where their eyes go first, and where they get stuck
Ask them to say out loud what the business should do next month
Fix the one thing that confused them, then test again

b.v: Do not add more objects to fill empty space. Empty space is what makes the screen readable. A dashboard with twenty charts is a data dump with a nice background.
Practice

Finish your one-screen dashboard: title, three KPI cards, one slicer, one chart and one small table. Click each city in turn and write the three totals on paper. For Lahore the sales card must read 3,900 and orders must read 2. Then run the stranger test on a family member.

day-10.t: Day 10 — Print, share and keep it safe

b.v: Today's goal

v: Protect formulas and lock the layout so readers cannot break it
Choose between PDF, xlsx and a shared link for each reader
Write a short read-me so the file survives without you

b.v: About 20 minutes. Your finished dashboard open and saved.

A good file dies when it is emailed with no explanation and one person overwrites a formula. Ten minutes of protection and one short note keep it alive for years, and keep your name on something that still works.
1) Lock the formulas, not the clicks

By default every cell is locked but the sheet is not protected, so locking does nothing. You must protect the sheet for it to matter. Leave the slicer cells and any input cell unlocked so the reader can still filter.

Protect the dashboard:|Select the cells the reader may change, for example a target cell|Format Cells, Protection, untick Locked|Review, then Protect Sheet, and set a password you will not forget|Tick the boxes that allow selecting cells and using filters

v: Protect Sheet = stops editing, allows the actions you tick
Allow Edit Ranges = lets one named block stay editable without the password
Read-only recommended = a gentle prompt when someone opens the file

b.v: 2) Send the right format

A PDF cannot be edited, so it is right for a manager or a WhatsApp group. An xlsx is right for a colleague who must refresh the data. A shared link is right for a team that edits together. Choose per person, not per habit.

v: PDF = fixed, prints the same everywhere, good for records
XLSX = editable, good for the person who updates the data
Link = live and shared, good for a team, weak if the internet is down

v.cap: A tiny read-me sheet. Two minutes to write, years of value.
rows: Sheet Data, rows 2 down, add new rows at the bottom
Paste new rows, press Refresh All, then check the total
Prepared by Sana, contact on WhatsApp

b.v: 3) Check before you send

Three checks take two minutes and save an embarrassing meeting. First, clear all filters. Second, confirm the grand total against your known number. Third, look at print preview and page one of the PDF.
A password you forget is a locked file you cannot open again. Keep the sheet password in your own record, and never protect a file you have not also saved a copy of without protection.
Practice

Protect your dashboard, leaving only the target cell editable. Export a one-page PDF. Add a read-me sheet with the five answers above. Finally, send the PDF to yourself on WhatsApp and open it on your phone, which is how most of your readers will see it.
